p.seg: The Parable of the Fool Eating Salt
Once upon a time, there was a fool
who went to someone else's house.
The host gave him food,
but he complained that it was bland and tasteless.
When the host heard this,
he added more salt for him.
Having obtained the salty deliciousness,
he thought to himself,
"The reason it's so delicious
is because of the salt.
If a little is like this,
how much more so with a lot?"
The fool, lacking wisdom,
then ate salt directly.
After eating it, his mouth was burning,
and it turned into a problem for him.
This is like those heretics
who hear that abstaining from food and drink can lead to enlightenment,
and immediately stop eating,
sometimes for seven days,
sometimes for fifteen days.
They only suffer from hunger,
which is of no benefit to the path.
Like that fool
who ate salt directly because it tasted good,
causing his mouth to burn,
this is also similar.
Once upon a time, there was a fool
who was going to host guests.
He wanted to gather milk
to prepare for the feast,
and he thought to himself:
"If I milk the cow little by little every day,
the milk will gradually increase,
but there will be no place to store it,
and it might even turn sour.
It's better to just store it in the cow's belly,
and when the feast is about to begin,
I'll milk it all at once."
Having thought this,
he tied up the mother cow and her calf,
each in a different place.
A month later,
he prepared the feast,
welcomed the guests,
and then led the cow over
to milk it,
but the milk had already dried up and was gone.
At that time, the guests were either angry or laughing.
The fool is also like this:
wanting to practice generosity,
he says,
"When I have a lot of wealth,
then I will give generously all at once."
Before he has accumulated it,
it might be seized by government officials, fire, or thieves,
or he might suddenly die
before he has time to give,
which is just like that.
Once upon a time, there was a fool
who had no hair on his head.
At that time, someone
hit him on the head with a pear,
even two or three times,
causing injuries and breaks all over.
At that time, this fool silently endured it,
not knowing to avoid it.
Someone nearby saw this
and said to him,
"Why don't you avoid it,
instead of staying there and getting hit,
causing your head to break?"
The fool replied,
"That person is arrogant and relies on his strength;
he is foolish and has no wisdom.
Seeing that I have no hair on my head,
he thought it was a stone,
and that's why he hit my head with a pear until it broke."
The person nearby said,
"You yourself are foolish.
How can you call him foolish?
If you weren't foolish,
why would you let him hit you,
even until your head breaks,
without knowing to run away?"
A *bhikkhu* is also like this:
unable to fully cultivate faith, discipline, learning, and wisdom,
he only focuses on his appearance
in order to attract offerings.
He is like that fool
who was hit on the head
but didn't know to avoid it,
even until he was injured and broken,
and instead called the other person foolish.
This *bhikkhu* is also like that.
Once upon a time, there was a fool
whose wife was beautiful
and whom he loved very much.
But the wife was unfaithful.
Later, she secretly had relations with another man,
and her adulterous desire grew strong.
She wanted to follow the other man
and leave her own husband.
So she secretly said to an old woman,
"After I leave,
you can bring a dead woman's corpse and put it in the house,
and tell my husband
that I have died."
Later, when her husband was away, the old woman
placed a dead corpse
in his house.
When her husband returned,
the old woman said,
"Your wife has died."
The husband immediately went to look,
believed it was his wife,
and cried in grief and remorse.
He piled up firewood and oil,
burned her bones,
put them in a bag,
and carried it with him day and night.
Later, the wife grew tired of the other man
and returned home,
saying to her husband,
"I am your wife."
The husband replied,
"My wife has been dead for a long time.
Who are you,
falsely claiming to be my wife?"
Even after two or three times,
he still didn't believe her.
This is like those heretics
who hear other people's false teachings
and become confused and attached,
considering them to be true
and never changing their minds.
Even if they hear the correct teachings,
they don't believe and accept them.
In the past, there was a person
who was foolish and lacked wisdom.
Extremely thirsty and needing water,
he saw the shimmering heat
and thought it was water.
He immediately ran after it
until he reached the Xīntóu River (辛頭河).
Having reached the river,
he looked at it but didn't drink.
Someone nearby said,
"You are thirsty and chasing after water,
but now that you've reached the water,
why don't you drink?"
The fool replied,
"If you can drink it all,
then I will drink it.
This water is extremely abundant
and cannot be drunk completely,
therefore I will not drink it."
At that time, everyone who heard his words laughed loudly.
This is like heretics who misunderstand the principles,
and because they cannot fully uphold the Buddha's precepts,
they refuse to accept them,
causing them to have no chance of attaining enlightenment in the future
and continuing to transmigrate in *saṃsāra*.
Like that fool
who didn't drink the water when he saw it
and was laughed at by everyone,
this is also similar.
Once upon a time, there was a fool
who raised seven children.
One of his children died first.
When this fool saw that his child had died,
he wanted to leave him in the house
and go away himself.
Someone nearby saw this
and said to him,
"Life and death are different paths.
You should quickly prepare the body
and take it to a distant place
to bury it.
How can you leave him here
and go away yourself?"
When the fool heard these words,
he immediately thought to himself,
"If I can't leave him here
and I have to bury him,
then I need to kill another child
to carry them on both ends of a pole,
so I can carry them more easily."
So he killed another one of his children
and carried them away
to bury them in the forest.
When people saw this,
they laughed deeply
and found it strange and unprecedented.
For example, a *bǐqiū*
secretly violates a precept,
fearing and reluctant to repent,
silently concealing it,
claiming to be pure.
Someone who knows this
will say to him:
"A renunciant guards the precepts
like protecting a bright pearl,
not allowing it to be flawed or lost.
How can you now violate what you have received and not repent?"
The one who broke the precept says:
"If I must repent,
I will commit more violations
and then confess everything."
Thereupon he breaks more precepts
and does many unwholesome deeds,
and then suddenly confesses.
This is like that foolish person
who, after one child died,
killed another.
This *bǐqiū* is also like this.
Once there was a person
who was handsome
and possessed wisdom,
and also had much money.
Everyone in the world praised him upon hearing of him.
At that time, a foolish person
saw this and
said, "He is my brother."
The reason for this was
that he had money
and would use it for those in need,
therefore he was his brother; when he saw him repaying debts, he said he was not his brother.
Those nearby said:
"You are a fool!
Why do you call him brother when you need his money?
And when he is in debt,
you say he is not your brother."
The fool replied:
"I recognize him as my brother because I want his money,
but he is not really my brother.
When he is in debt,
I say he is not my brother."
People who heard this
could not help but laugh.
It is like those heretics,
who, upon hearing the Buddha's good words,
greedily steal and use them,
thinking they are their own.
Even when others teach and urge them to practice,
they refuse to practice,
and say:
"For the sake of profit and offerings,
they take the Buddha's words
to convert beings,
but there is nothing substantial,
why should we practice?"
It is like the foolish person
who, for the sake of getting money,
said he was his brother,
and when he was in debt,
said he was not his brother.
This is also like that.
In the past, there was a mountain bandit
who stole from the king's treasury
and fled far away.
At that time, the king sent people to search in all directions and they captured him,
bringing him to the king's presence.
The king then questioned him about where he got the clothes he was wearing.
The mountain bandit replied:
"These clothes are from my ancestors."
The king ordered him to put on the clothes.
Because they were not originally the mountain bandit's,
he did not know how to wear them.
He put what should be on his hands on his feet,
and what should be on his waist on his head.
Seeing the thief,
the king gathered his ministers
to discuss this matter together,
and said to them:
"If these clothes have been passed down from your ancestors,
you should know how to wear them.
Why do you wear them upside down,
using the top as the bottom?
Because you do not know how to wear them,
it is certain that you stole these clothes;
they are not your own."
To borrow this as an analogy,
the king is like the Buddha,
the treasury is like the Dharma,
the foolish bandit is like the heretics,
who secretly listen to the Buddha's Dharma
and attach it to their own teachings,
thinking it is their own.
However, because they do not understand it,
they arrange the Buddha's Dharma
in a confused and disordered way,
not knowing the true nature of the Dharma.
It is like the mountain bandit
who obtained the king's precious clothes,
but did not recognize the proper order
and wore them upside down,
so it is also like that.
In the past, there was a person
who, in a crowd, praised his father's virtues,
saying:
"My father is kind and benevolent,
he does not harm or steal,
he speaks truthfully
and practices generosity."
At that time, a foolish person
heard this and
thought to himself:
"My father's virtue surpasses your father's."
People asked:
"What virtues does he have?
Please tell us about it."
The fool replied:
"My father has abstained from lust since he was young,
and has never been defiled."
The crowd said:
"If he abstained from lust,
how were you born?"
He was greatly laughed at by the people of the time.
It is like the ignorant people of the world,
who want to praise someone's virtues
but do not know the truth,
and instead cause defamation.
Like that fool,
who intended to praise his father
but whose words became a fault,
so it is also like that.
In the past, there was a wealthy fool
who was ignorant and knew nothing.
He went to another wealthy family's house
and saw a three-story building,
tall, spacious, and beautifully decorated,
open, airy, and bright.
His heart filled with longing
and he thought:
"I have money
no less than they do,
why haven't I built such a building?"
He immediately called a carpenter
and asked:
"Can you build a fine house like that one?"
The carpenter replied:
"I built it."
He immediately said:
"Now build me a building like that one."
At that time, the carpenter immediately surveyed the land, piled up bricks, and started building the house.
The fool saw him piling up bricks and building the house,
but he was still doubtful
and could not understand.
He asked:
"What are you trying to build?"
The carpenter replied:
"Building a three-story house."
The fool said again:
"I don't want the lower two stories,
first build the top story for me."
The carpenter replied:
"That is impossible.
How can you build the second story without building the lowest story?
If you don't build the second story,
how can you build the third story?"
The fool insisted:
"I don't need the lower two stories now,
you must build the top one for me."
When people heard this,
they were surprised and laughed,
saying:
"How can you build the top story
without building the first story?"
It is like the *shìzūn*'s four kinds of disciples
who do not diligently cultivate respect for the Three Jewels,
are lazy and slothful,
and want to attain the fruits of the path,
and say:
"I don't need the other three lower fruits,
I only seek to attain the *āluóhàn* fruit."
They are also ridiculed by the people of the time,
like that fool, there is no difference.
Once there was a *pólómén*
who claimed to be very knowledgeable,
and was proficient in all kinds of astrology and skills.
Relying on this,
he wanted to show off his virtues,
so he went to another country,
holding a child and crying.
Someone asked the *pólómén*:
"Why are you crying?"
The *póluómén* said:
"This child will die in seven days.
I pity his premature death,
so I am crying about it."
The people at the time said:
"Human life is hard to predict.
Calculations often go wrong.
Suppose he doesn't die in seven days;
why are you crying in advance?"
The *póluómén* said:
"The sun and moon may be darkened,
the stars may fall,
but what I have foretold will never be wrong."
For the sake of fame and profit,
on the seventh day,
he killed his own son
to prove his words.
After seven days, the people heard of the child's death
and all sighed, saying:
"He is truly wise;
what he said was not wrong."
They were convinced in their hearts
and came to pay their respects.
It is like the Buddha's four kinds of disciples,
who, for the sake of profit and support,
claim to have attained the Dao.
They have the Dharma of foolish people,
killing good men
and falsely displaying kindness.
Thus, they will suffer endlessly in the future,
like the *póluómén* who killed his son to verify his words and delude the world.
Once upon a time, there was a foolish man
who was boiling black *shímì*.
A wealthy man
came to his house.
Then this foolish man thought:
"I should take some black *shímì* syrup and give it to this wealthy man."
So he added a little water
and put it in the fire.
He then fanned it over the fire
hoping to cool it down.
A person nearby said:
"If you don't stop the fire,
and keep fanning it,
how will it cool down?"
At that time, everyone laughed.
It is like the heretics who do not extinguish the burning fire of afflictions,
but do a little ascetic practice,
lying on thorny bushes,
and scorching their bodies with five heats,
hoping for the cool and tranquil path.
There is no such possibility.
They only invite ridicule from the wise,
suffering in the present
and bringing disaster to future kalpas.
In the past, there was a person sitting in a house with many people,
praising an outsider's extremely good virtue,
"He only has two faults:
one is that he likes to be angry,
and the other is that he is hasty in doing things."
At that time, this person was passing by outside the door,
heard these words,
and became angry.
He immediately entered the house
and seized the person who had spoken of his foolishness and wickedness,
and beat him with his hands.
The people nearby asked:
"Why are you beating him?"
The man replied:
"When have I ever liked to be angry or been hasty?
But this person said, 'I like to be angry and am hasty in doing things.'
That is why I am beating him."
The people nearby said:
"Your liking to be angry and being hasty is now immediately evident;
how can you deny it?"
To become resentful and blame others for pointing out one's faults
is deeply foolish and bewildering to everyone.
It is like a drunken man in the world,
indulging in and addicted to alcohol,
engaging in all kinds of unrestrained behavior,
and becoming even more resentful
when someone scolds him.
He painstakingly seeks evidence
to justify himself.
Like this foolish man,
he avoids hearing his own faults,
and when he hears others talking about them,
he wants to beat them.
Once upon a time, there was a merchant
who wanted to enter the great sea.
The way to enter the great sea requires a guide,
and only then can one go.
So he searched and found a guide.
Having found him,
they set off together
into the wilderness.
There was a heavenly shrine
that required a human sacrifice to pass through.
Thereupon, all the merchants discussed together, saying:
"We are all relatives and friends;
how can we kill each other?
Only this guide can be used to sacrifice to the heavens."
So they killed the guide
to use him as a sacrifice.
After the sacrifice to the heavens was completed,
they lost their way
and did not know where to go,
and they all died in poverty and distress.
All the people in the world are also like this.
If they want to enter the sea of Dharma to obtain its treasures,
they should cultivate good deeds and make them their guide.
If they destroy good deeds,
they will never escape the wilderness of birth and death,
passing through the three evil destinies
and suffering for a long time,
like those merchants
who wanted to enter the great sea,
killed their guide,
lost their way,
and ultimately died in distress.
Once upon a time, a king
had a daughter born,
"Give me medicine
to make her grow up quickly."
The doctor replied:
"I have good medicine that can make her grow up immediately,
but I don't have it right now.
I need to search for it.
Before I get the medicine,
the king must not look at her.
Wait until I give her the medicine
and then show her to the king."
Thereupon, he went far away to get the medicine
for twelve years.
He got the medicine and came back
and gave it to the girl to take.
He then showed her to the king.
The king was happy
and thought to himself:
"He is truly a good doctor.
He gave my daughter medicine
that made her grow up so quickly."
He immediately ordered his attendants to give him treasures.
At that time, everyone laughed at the king's ignorance,
for not understanding how to calculate the years since she was born,
and seeing that she had grown up,
they thought it was the power of the medicine.
The people of the world are also like this.
They go to a good teacher
and say to him:
"I want to seek the Dao.
I hope to be taught
so that I can attain it immediately."
The good teacher, by skillful means, teaches them to sit in meditation and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination,
gradually accumulating merits
and attaining Arhatship.
They are overjoyed and happy
and say:
"How wonderful, great master!
You can quickly enable me to realize the most wonderful Dharma."
Once upon a time, there were two people
and made a vow, saying:
"The one who plants well will be rewarded,
and the one who does not plant well
will be severely punished."
At that time, one of the two thought:
"Sugarcane is very sweet.
If I squeeze out the juice
and irrigate the sugarcane trees with it,
the sweetness will surely be greater,
and I will be better than him."
So he squeezed the sugarcane
and used the juice to irrigate them,
hoping for better flavor,
but instead ruined the seeds.
All the sugarcane was lost.
The people of the world are also like this.
They want to seek good fortune,
but rely on their own wealth and power,
and display their powerful influence,
oppressing the lower people,
plundering their property,
and using it to make merit,
hoping for good results.
They do not know that in the future they will instead suffer from misfortune,
like squeezing sugarcane,
and both will be lost.
Once there was a merchant
who lent someone half a qián,
and for a long time, he was not repaid,
so he went to collect the debt.
There was a large river in front of him,
and he hired someone for two qián
to cross it.
When he arrived, he went to collect the debt
but could not find the person.
He returned to cross the river
and hired someone again for two qián.
For a debt of half a qián, he lost four qián,
and was also exhausted from the journey.
The debt was very small,
but the loss was extremely large,
and indeed he was laughed at by everyone.
The people of the world are also like this,
seeking small fame and profit
that leads to the destruction of great deeds,
indulging themselves
and disregarding propriety and righteousness,
incurring a bad reputation now
and receiving bitter retribution later.
In the past, there was a man
who was poor and destitute,
working for the king.
As the days and months passed,
his body became thin and weak.
The king, seeing him, took pity
and gave him a dead camel.
The poor man, having received it,
immediately began to skin it.
Disliking the dullness of his knife,
he sought a stone to sharpen it on.
He found a grindstone upstairs,
sharpened the knife to make it sharp,
and came downstairs to skin the camel.
He went back and forth many times to sharpen the knife.
Later, he became weary
and unwilling to go upstairs so many times.
He hung the camel upstairs
and sharpened the knife next to the stone,
which was deeply ridiculed by everyone.
It is like a foolish person
destroying precepts,
taking much money
to use for cultivating blessings,
hoping to be reborn in heaven,
like hanging the camel upstairs to sharpen the knife,
putting in much effort
but gaining very little.
Once, someone was crossing the sea by boat
and lost a silver hairpin
that fell into the water.
He immediately thought:
"I will mark the water where it fell,
leave it,
and retrieve it later."
After traveling for two months,
he arrived at the various kingdoms of Shīzǐ,
and saw a river.
He entered it
to look for the hairpin he had lost.
People asked him,
"What do you intend to do?"
He replied,
"I lost a hairpin earlier
and now I want to find it."
They asked,
"Where did you lose it?"
He replied,
"I lost it when I first entered the sea."
Again they asked,
"How long ago did you lose it?"
He said,
"I lost it two months ago."
They asked,
"You lost it two months ago,
how can you look for it here?"
He replied,
"When I lost the hairpin,
I marked the water.
The water I marked is no different from this water,
therefore I am looking for it here."
Again they asked,
"Although the water is not different,
you lost it back then
over there,
and now you are looking for it here,
how can you find it?"
At that time, everyone laughed loudly.
It is also like non-Buddhist paths
not practicing correct conduct,
amidst similar good deeds, calculating suffering,
in order to seek liberation,
like a foolish person
losing a hairpin over there
and looking for it here.
Once there was a man
who spoke of the king's faults,
and said:
"The king is very tyrannical
and governs without reason."
The king heard these words
and became very angry,
and without thoroughly investigating who said these words,
believing flattering people,
he seized a virtuous minister,
ordered his back to be skinned
and a hundred liǎng of flesh taken.
Someone proved that he did not say these words.
The king then regretted it,
and sought a thousand liǎng of flesh
to use to repair his back.
At night, he groaned
with great suffering.
The king heard his voice
and asked,
"Why are you suffering?
I took a hundred liǎng from you,
and gave you ten times that amount,
is that not enough?
Why are you suffering?"
The person beside him replied,
"Great King!
Like cutting off a child's head,
even if you get a thousand heads
it will not prevent the child's death.
Even if you get ten times the amount of flesh,
it will not prevent the suffering."
Foolish people are also like this,
not fearing the afterlife,
thirsting for present pleasures,
afflicting sentient beings,
exploiting the common people,
gaining much wealth,
hoping to extinguish sins
and gain blessings.
It is like that king
cutting a person's back,
taking a person's flesh,
and using the remaining flesh to repair it,
hoping to make it not hurt,
which is impossible.
In the past, there was a woman
who had only one child
and wanted to have another child.
She asked other women,
"Who can make me have another child?"
An old woman told this woman,
"I can make it possible for you to have another child,
you must sacrifice to the heavens."
She asked the old woman,
"What is needed for the sacrifice?"
The old woman said,
"Kill your child,
take its blood to sacrifice to the heavens,
and you will surely have more children."
At that time, this woman followed her words and wanted to kill her child.
A wise person nearby
ridiculed and scolded her:
"Foolish and ignorant,
to such an extent!
Can a child that is not yet born necessarily be obtained?
Yet you kill the child you have now."
Foolish people are also like this,
throwing themselves into a fire pit for the sake of unborn pleasures,
harming their bodies in various ways
in order to be reborn in heaven.
*Bǎiyù Jīng*, Volume 1 [Preface] Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in Wángshěchéng,
in the Zhúfēng Yuán in the Qùefēng, with thirty-six thousand great *Bǐqiū*, *Púsà Mòhēsà*, and the eight divisions.
At that time, there were five hundred heretical Brahmins in the assembly,
who arose from their seats
and said to the Buddha:
"We have heard that the Buddha's path is vast and profound,
and no one can reach it,
therefore we have come to inquire,
we hope you will explain it."
The Buddha said, "Very good."
They asked, "Is the world existent or nonexistent?"
He replied,
"It is both existent and nonexistent."
The Brahmins said,
"If it is existent now, how can you say it is nonexistent?
If it is nonexistent now, how can you say it is existent?"
He replied,
"Those who are alive are said to be existent,
those who are dead are said to be nonexistent,
therefore I say
it is sometimes existent and sometimes nonexistent."
They asked,
"From where do people come?"
He replied,
"People come from grain."
They asked,
"From where does the five grains come?"
He replied,
"The five grains come from the four great elements: earth, water, fire, and wind."
Question:
"From where do the four great elements, fire and wind, arise?"
Answer:
"The four great elements, fire and wind, arise from emptiness."
Question:
"From where does emptiness arise?"
Answer:
"It arises from nothingness."
Question:
"From where does nothingness arise?"
Answer:
"It arises from spontaneity (zìrán)."
Question:
"From where does spontaneity arise?"
Answer:
"It arises from *nirvāṇa* (níhuán)."
Question:
"From where does *nirvāṇa* arise?"
The Buddha said:
"Why do you ask such a profound
question?
*Nirvāṇa* is the dharma of neither birth nor death."
Question:
"Has the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*?"
Answer:
"I have not yet entered *nirvāṇa*."
"If you have not yet entered *nirvāṇa*,
how do you know that *nirvāṇa* is eternally blissful?"
The Buddha said:
"I will now ask you,
are sentient beings in the world suffering or enjoying?"
Answer:
"Sentient beings suffer greatly."
The Buddha said:
"What do you mean by suffering?"
Answer:
"I see sentient beings suffer unbearable pain at the time of death,
therefore I know the suffering of death."
The Buddha said:
"You have not died
and yet you know the suffering of death;
I see the Buddhas of the ten directions neither born nor dying,
therefore I know *nirvāṇa* is eternally blissful."
Five hundred Brahmins opened their hearts and minds,
sought to receive the five precepts,
realized the fruit of *Srotaāpanna* (xūtuóhuán guǒ),
and sat again as before.
The Buddha said:
"Listen carefully!
Now I will explain various parables for you extensively."

Once upon a time, there was the son of a wealthy man
who entered the sea to obtain agarwood.
He accumulated it for many years,
finally obtaining a cartload
which he brought home.
He went to the market to sell it,
but because it was expensive,
no one bought it.
After many days, he was unable to sell it,
and he became weary
and distressed.
Seeing that people were selling charcoal and quickly making sales,
he had the thought:
"It would be better to burn it and make charcoal,
so that it can be sold quickly."
He immediately burned it into charcoal.
He went to the market to sell it,
but did not get even half the value of a cartload of charcoal.
Foolish people in the world are also like this.
With limitless skillful means, they diligently cultivate and advance,
aspiring to seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because it is difficult to attain,
they develop a retreating mind.
"It would be better to generate the aspiration to seek the fruit of a *Śrāvaka* (shēngwén guǒ), quickly cut off birth and death, and become an *Arhat* (āluóhàn)."
Once upon a time, there was a thief
who entered the house of a rich family
and stole brocade.
He immediately used it to wrap old, tattered woolen cloth and various other items,
which was laughed at by wise people.
Foolish people in the world are also like this.
Having already developed faith
and entered the Buddha Dharma,
cultivating good dharmas and various merits,
they break the pure precepts and various merits
due to greed for profit,
which is laughed at by the world.
It is also like this.
Once upon a time, there was a foolish person
who ate raw sesame seeds
and thought they were not good.
He roasted them and ate them, and they were good.
He then had the thought:
"It would be better to roast them and then sow them,
so that I can obtain better ones later."
He then roasted them and sowed them,
but they never sprouted.
People in the world are also like this.
They think that the *Bodhisattva's* (púsà) cultivation over countless *kalpas* (jié),
the cause of difficult practices and ascetic practices,
is unpleasant.
They then have the thought:
"It would be better to become an *Arhat* (āluóhàn),
quickly cut off birth and death,
and its merit is very easy."
Later, wanting to seek the fruit of Buddhahood,
it can never be obtained,
like those roasted seeds
which can no longer sprout.
Foolish people in the world are also like this.
Once upon a time, there was a person
who needed fire and cold water for some matter.
He then put out the fire
and used a washing vessel to hold water
and placed it on the fire.
Later, wanting to take fire,
the fire was completely extinguished.
Wanting to take cold water,
the water was hot again.
He lost both fire and cold water.
People in the world are also like this.
Entering the Buddha Dharma,
renouncing the household life and seeking the Way,
having already renounced the household life,
they still think of their wives, children, relatives, worldly affairs, and the pleasures of the five desires.
Because of this, they lose the fire of their merit and the water of upholding the precepts.
People who are attached to desires are also like this.
Once upon a time, there was a person
who wanted to gain the king's favor.
He asked other people,
"How can I obtain it?"
Someone said:
"If you want to gain the king's favor,
you should imitate the king's appearance."
This person then went to the king's place.
Seeing the king's eye twitch, he then imitated the king's twitch.
The king asked him:
"Are you sick?
Or are you affected by wind?
Why are your eyes twitching?"
The person answered the king:
"I am not sick,
nor am I affected by wind.
I want to gain the king's favor.
Seeing the king's eye twitch,
therefore I imitate the king."
The king, hearing these words,
became very angry.
He then ordered people to inflict various kinds of harm
and banished him from the country.
People in the world are also like this.
In the Buddha Dharma, the King, wanting to become close,
they seek good dharmas
to increase themselves.
Having become close,
they do not understand that the *Tathāgata* (rúlái), the Dharma King, for the sake of sentient beings,
manifests shortcomings through various skillful means.
Or hearing his Dharma,
seeing that there are incorrect words and phrases,
they then give rise to criticism and slander,
imitating what is not right.
Because of this,
in the Buddha Dharma they forever lose their goodness
and fall into the three evil realms,
like that person who imitated the king, it is also like this.
Once upon a time, there was a man
who was whipped by the king.
After being whipped,
he used horse dung to smear
the wounds, hoping they would heal quickly.
A foolish man saw this
and was delighted,
saying,
"I have definitely found a way to treat sores!"
Immediately he went home
and said to his son,
"Whip my back,
I have a good method
and I want to try it now."
The son whipped his back,
and he smeared it with horse dung,
thinking it was a clever trick.
The people of the world are like this.
Hearing someone say
that practicing impurity meditation
can remove the sores of the five aggregates,
they say,
"I want to contemplate female beauty and the five desires."
Without seeing impurity,
they are instead confused by female beauty,
transmigrating in birth and death
and falling into hell.
The foolish people of the world are also like this.
Once upon a time, there was a man
whose wife was beautiful
except for her ugly nose.
The man went out
and saw another woman whose face was beautiful
and whose nose was very good.
He thought,
"Wouldn't it be good if I could cut off her nose
and put it on my wife's face?"
So he cut off the other woman's nose
and brought it home.
He hurriedly called out to his wife,
"Come out quickly,
I have a good nose for you!"
His wife came out,
and he immediately cut off her nose,
then tried to put the other nose on his wife's face.
It didn't attach,
and she also lost her original nose,
causing his wife great pain for nothing.
The foolish people of the world are also like this.
Hearing that other long-standing *shāmén* ān *póluómén* (沙門婆羅門) have great fame and virtue
and are respected by the world
and receive great offerings,
they think,
"I will become no different from them."
They falsely pretend
and lie about having virtue.
They lose their benefits
and damage their conduct.
Like cutting off someone else's nose,
they only harm themselves in vain.
The foolish people of the world are also like this.
Once upon a time, there was a man
who was poor and destitute.
He worked for others
and received a coarse hemp garment
which he wore.
Someone saw him
and said to him,
"You are of noble lineage,
the son of a noble,
why are you wearing this coarse, worn-out hemp garment?
I will teach you now,
I will make you obtain excellent clothes,
follow my words
and I will never deceive you."
The poor man was delighted
and respectfully followed his words.
The man then lit a fire in front of him
and said to the poor man,
"Now you can take off this coarse hemp garment
and put it in the fire.
At this burning place, I will make you obtain excellent and admirable clothing."
The poor man immediately took it off and put it in the fire.
After it was burned,
he searched for admirable clothing at the fire
but found nothing.
The people of the world are also like this.
From past lives, they cultivate various good deeds
and obtain this human body.
They should protect it, advance in virtue, and cultivate their karma,
but they are deceived by heretical *wàidào* (外道) evil enchantresses:
"Now you should believe my words
and practice various ascetic practices,
jump off cliffs and into fire.
After abandoning this body,
you will be born in the Brahma Heaven
and enjoy happiness for a long time."
They then follow their words
and immediately abandon their lives.
After dying,
they fall into hell
and suffer all kinds of pain.
They lose their human body
and gain nothing in vain,
just like that poor man.
The foolish people of the world are also like this.
Once upon a time, there was a man
who was skilled at herding sheep.
His sheep multiplied
to tens of millions.
He was extremely stingy
and unwilling to spend anything.
At that time, there was a man
who was good at deception.
He devised a plan
to become close friends with him
and said to him,
"I am now extremely close to you,
we are as one
and there is no difference between us.
I know there is a good woman in that family,
I will seek her for you
to be your wife."
The sheep herder
was delighted to hear this
and gave him many sheep and other valuables.
The man then said,
"Your wife has already given birth to a son today."
The sheep herder had not seen his wife,
but hearing that she had given birth
he was overjoyed
and gave him more things.
Later, the man said to him again,
"Your son has died after being born."
The sheep herder, hearing these words,
wept and sobbed uncontrollably.
The people of the world are also like this.
They cultivate much learning,
but they hoard their knowledge for fame and profit,
unwilling to teach and explain it to others.
They are deceived and deluded by this leaking body
and falsely expect worldly pleasures.
Like a wife and children being deceived by them,
they lose their good deeds.
Later, they lose their lives and wealth,
and weep greatly,
giving rise to their sorrow and suffering,
just like that sheep herder.
Once upon a time, there was a *póluómén* (婆羅門) teacher
who wanted to hold a large gathering.
He said to his disciple,
"I need clay pots for the gathering,
you can hire a potter and find them in the market for me."
At that time, the disciple went to the potter's house.
At that time, there was a man
whose donkey was carrying clay pots
to the market to sell.
In a short time, the donkey broke all of them.
He returned home
weeping and annoyed.
The disciple saw this
and asked him,
"Why are you so sad and annoyed?"
The man replied,
"I worked hard and accumulated for many years to make these pots.
I went to the market to sell them,
but this wretched donkey broke all my pots in a short time.
That is why I am annoyed."
At that time, the disciple, having seen and heard this,
said happily,
"This donkey is a good thing.
It can break what took a long time to make in a short time.
I will buy this donkey now."
The potter was delighted
and immediately sold it to him.
He rode it home.
The teacher asked him,
"Why didn't you bring the potter here,
but instead brought this donkey?"
The disciple replied,
"This donkey is better than the potter.
The potter's pots, which took a long time to make, it can break in a short time."
At that time, the teacher said,
"You are very foolish and have no wisdom!
This donkey can only break things now.
Even if it lived for a hundred years, it could not make one pot."
The people of the world are also like this.
Although they receive offerings from people for thousands of years,
they do not repay them at all.
They always cause harm
and never benefit.
The ungrateful people are also like this.
In the past, there were two merchants,
who traveled together to trade.
One sold genuine gold,
and the other sold _dōuluó mián_ (kapok).
Someone wanted to buy the genuine gold
and burned it to test it.
The second merchant then secretly stole the gold being burned,
wrapped it in _dōuluó mián_,
but because the gold was hot, the _mián_ was completely burned away,
and the truth was revealed, so both things were lost.
It is like those heretics
who steal the Buddha's teachings
and put them into their own teachings,
falsely claiming them as their own
when they are not the Buddha's teachings.
Because of this,
their heretical scriptures are burned and destroyed
and do not circulate in the world.
It is like stealing gold;
the whole affair is exposed,
and it is the same way.
In the past, there was a king
who had a good tree
that was tall and broad,
destined to produce superior fruit
that was fragrant and sweet.
At that time, a man
came to the king's place.
The king said to him,
"This tree
will bear beautiful fruit;
can you eat it?"
He immediately answered the king, saying,
"This tree is tall and broad;
even if I want to eat it, how can I obtain it?"
So he cut down the tree
hoping to get its fruit,
but he obtained nothing
and only labored in vain.
Later, he wanted to erect it again,
but the tree was already withered and dead
and had no way to live.
The people of the world are also like this.
The _Rúlái_ (Tathāgata) Dharma King has a tree of precepts that can produce superior fruit.
If one's mind desires happiness
and wants to obtain the fruit to eat,
one should uphold the precepts
and cultivate various meritorious deeds.
But if one does not understand expedient means,
but instead destroys the precepts,
it is like felling the tree.
Even if one wants to revive it,
it is impossible to obtain.
A person who breaks the precepts is also like this.
In the past, there was a village
five _yóuxún_ (leagues) away from the royal city.
In the village, there was good, beautiful water.
The king ordered the villagers to send the beautiful water to him daily.
The villagers were tired and weary
and all wanted to move away from this village.
At that time, the village chief said to the people,
"Do not go!
I will report to the king for you,
to change five _yóuxún_ to three _yóuxún_,
so that you can travel back and forth without being tired."
He immediately went to report to the king.
The king changed it
to three _yóuxún_.
When the people heard this,
they were very happy.
Someone said,
"This is still the original five _yóuxún_;
there is no difference."
Although they heard this,
because they believed the king's words,
they ultimately would not give up.

The people of the world are also like this: cultivating the correct Dharma to cross the five paths towards the city of _Nièpán_ (Nirvana), their minds become weary and they want to abandon it, halting their progress in _shēngsǐ_ (samsara) and being unable to advance further. The _Rúlái_ (Tathāgata) Dharma King has great expedient means, and in the One Vehicle Dharma, he separately speaks of the Three Vehicles.
People of the Small Vehicle hear this and rejoice,
thinking it is easy to practice.
They cultivate good deeds and advance in virtue,
seeking to cross over _shēngsǐ_ (samsara).
Later, they hear people say,
"There are no Three Vehicles;
it is originally One Vehicle."
Because they believe the Buddha's words,
they ultimately will not give up,
just like those villagers.
It is also like that.
In the past, there was a man
who was poor and destitute,
owing many people debts
that he could not repay.
He immediately fled
to an empty, open place.
He encountered a chest, full of treasures,
with a bright mirror
placed on top of the treasures,
covered with a lid.
When the poor man saw it,
his heart was greatly pleased.
He immediately opened it,
saw the person in the mirror,
and became frightened.
He put his palms together and said,
"I thought it was an empty chest
with nothing at all.
I didn't know you were in this chest.
Please don't be angry."
Ordinary people are also like this,
impoverished by limitless afflictions,
and entangled by the debt collectors of the _shēngsǐ_ (samsara) demon king.
Wanting to avoid _shēngsǐ_ (samsara),
they enter the Buddha's Dharma,
cultivate good deeds,
and perform various meritorious deeds.
It is like encountering a treasure chest,
but they are confused and misled by the mirror of self-view,
falsely seeing that there is a self.
They immediately seal it shut,
thinking it is real.
Thereupon, they fall
and lose all their meritorious deeds, _chándìng_ (dhyana), the path, the unconditioned good,
and all the results of the Three Vehicle path.
It is like that foolish man
who abandons the treasure chest;
those attached to self-view are also like this.
In the past, there was a man
who entered the mountains to study the Way
and attained the five _tōng_ (supernatural powers) of an immortal.
With his heavenly eye, he could see clearly
all the hidden treasures and various jewels in the ground.
When the king heard of this,
his heart was greatly pleased.
He then said to his ministers,
"How can we keep this person in my kingdom
and not let him go elsewhere?
So that my treasury will have more jewels."
A foolish minister
immediately went
and gouged out the eyes of the immortal
and brought them to report to the king:
"Your minister has gouged out his eyes;
he can no longer leave
and will always reside in this kingdom."
The king said to the minister,
"The reason I wanted to keep the immortal was
because he could see all the hidden treasures in the ground.
Now that you have destroyed his eyes,
what use is he anymore?"
The people of the world are also like this.
Seeing others practicing _tóutuó_ (asceticism), suffering and practicing in the mountains, forests, wilderness, cemeteries, and under trees,
cultivating the Four Foundations of Mindfulness and the Contemplation of Impurity,
they forcibly bring them
to their homes, making various offerings,
destroying their good Dharma,
causing the path to not be accomplished,
losing their Dharma eyes.
Having already lost its benefit,
there is nothing to gain,
like that foolish minister
who vainly destroyed the eyes of another.
In the past, there was a man
who had two hundred and fifty cows,
who regularly drove them to water and grass
to feed them according to the season.
At that time, a tiger
ate one of the cows.
Then, the owner of the cows immediately thought,
"Having already lost one cow,
they are not complete.
What use are these cows?"
He immediately drove them to a deep pit with high banks,
pushed them into the bottom of the pit,
and killed them all.
Ordinary foolish people are also like this:
receiving and upholding the complete precepts of the _Rúlái_ (Tathāgata).
If they violate one precept, they do not feel shame or purify it through repentance.
They then think,
"I have already broken one precept.
Since it is not complete,
what is the use of upholding them?"
They break everything
without leaving a single one,
like that foolish man
who killed all his cows
without leaving a single one.
In the past, there was a man
who was thirsty from traveling.
He saw clear, pure water in a wooden tube,
approached it, and drank.
Having drunk his fill,
he immediately raised his hand
and said to the wooden tube,
"I have finished drinking;
water, do not come anymore."
Although he said this,
the water flowed as before.
Then, in anger, he said:
"I have already finished drinking,
I told you not to come,
why did you come?"
Someone saw this and said:
"You are extremely foolish,
without any wisdom!
Why don't you go away,
since you told them not to come?"
So they pulled him away
and dragged him to another place.
People in the world are also like this,
thirsting for the love of birth and death,
drinking the salty water of the five desires.
Once they are exhausted and weary of the five desires,
like someone who has drunk his fill,
they then say:
"You forms, sounds, smells, tastes, do not come again to make me see you."
However, these five desires continue without ceasing,
and once they see them again,
they become angry again:
"I told you to quickly disappear,
do not arise again,
why do you come
and make me see you?"
Then a wise person says to them:
"If you want to be free from them,
you should restrain your six senses,
close off your mind,
and if deluded thoughts do not arise,
then you will be liberated.
Why is it necessary not to see them,
wanting to prevent them from arising?"
They are no different from that foolish person drinking water.
Once upon a time, there was a man
who went to another's house,
and saw that the walls of the house were plastered and repaired,
and the ground was level and
very clean and good.
He asked, saying:
"What did you mix with the plaster to make it so good?"
The owner replied:
"We used rice grain
and bran soaked in water until soft,
and mixed it with mud to plaster the walls,
and that's how it became like this."
The fool then had this thought:
"If using pure rice
and bran is good, it would be better to combine them than to use rice alone,
then the walls will be whiter
and the mud will be more level and good."
So he used rice grain mixed with mud
and plastered the walls with it,
hoping to make them level,
but instead they became even more uneven,
and the walls all cracked.
He wasted the rice grain
and gained no benefit at all,
it would have been better to give it away as charity,
then he could have gained merit.
Ordinary people are also like this,
hearing the saints preach the Dharma
and practice various good deeds,
so that after abandoning this body,
they can be reborn in the heavens and attain liberation,
they then commit suicide
hoping to be reborn in the heavens and attain liberation,
but they only waste themselves in vain
and gain nothing at all,
like that foolish person.
Once upon a time, there was a man
who had no hair on his head,
so he suffered greatly from the cold in winter
and from the heat in summer,
and was also bitten by mosquitoes and gadflies,
suffering annoyance day and night,
and found it very painful.
There was a doctor
who had many remedies,
and this bald man went to his place,
and said to the doctor:
"I beg you, great master, to cure me."
This doctor was also bald,
so he immediately took off his hat and showed it
and said to him:
"I also suffer from this
and find it painful,
if I could cure it
and get it cured,
I should first cure myself
to remove the affliction."
People in the world are also like this,
afflicted by birth, old age, sickness, and death,
wanting to seek a place of longevity and immortality,
hearing that there are *shāmén* and *bāluómén* and other good doctors in the world who can cure all kinds of illnesses,
they then go to their places
and say to them:
"I beg you to remove from me the affliction of impermanent birth and death,
so that I may always dwell in peace and happiness
and exist forever without change."
The *bāluómén* then reply:
"I also suffer from this impermanent birth, old age, sickness, and death,
and have sought in various ways for a place of lasting existence, but have never been able to find it.
If I could make you obtain it now,
I should first obtain it myself,
and then you would also obtain it."
Like that man suffering from baldness,
he only tires himself out in vain
and cannot be cured.
Once upon a time, there were two *píshězhē* ghosts,
who shared one box, one staff, and one pair of clogs.
The two ghosts argued
and each wanted to get them,
the two ghosts were in turmoil
and could not settle it all day.
Then a man
came and saw them
and asked them:
"What is so strange about this box, staff, and clogs?
That you are arguing
and so angry?"
The two ghosts replied:
"This box of mine can produce all kinds of clothes, food, bedding, and other necessities, all of which come from it.
If you hold this staff, your enemies will submit and dare not argue with you.
If you wear these clogs, you can fly without hindrance."
When this man heard this,
he said to the ghosts:
"You go a little further away,
and I will divide them equally for you."
When the ghosts heard this,
they immediately moved away.
The man immediately embraced the box, grabbed the staff, put on the clogs, and flew away,
the two ghosts were stunned
and gained nothing at all.
The man said to the ghosts:
"I have already taken what you were arguing about,
now I will make it so that you no longer have anything to argue about."
*Píshězhē* are metaphors for all demons and external paths.
Giving alms is like the box,
the necessities for humans, gods, and the five paths all come from it.
*Chán* meditation is like the staff,
subduing the demon enemies and the thieves of affliction.
Upholding the precepts is like the clogs,
surely ascending to the realms of humans and gods.
The demons and externalists fighting for the box are a metaphor for strongly seeking rewards in the realm of outflows,
but gaining nothing at all.
If one can cultivate good deeds and give alms, uphold the precepts, and practice *chán* meditation,
then one can be freed from suffering
and attain the fruit of the Path.
