Traveling merchants
met on the road, and a camel suddenly died.
The camel was loaded with many treasures, soft fine woolen fabrics, and various miscellaneous items.
After the camel died,
they skinned it.
The merchant leader abandoned the journey
and sat two disciples
down and said to them:
"Take good care of the camel skin,
don't let it get wet and rot."
Later, it rained,
and the two stubborn and foolish disciples
covered the skin with all the good woolen fabrics,
and all the woolen fabrics rotted and were ruined.
The value of the skin and the woolen fabrics was naturally vastly different.
Because of their foolishness, they covered the skin with the woolen fabrics.
People in the world are also like this,
those who do not kill are like white woolen fabric,
the camel skin is a metaphor for wealth and goods,
the rain causing dampness and rot is a metaphor for carelessness ruining good deeds.
The precept against killing is the most supreme and wonderful cause of the Buddha's Dharma body,
yet they cannot cultivate it.
Instead, they use wealth to build various pagodas and temples
and make offerings to the monastic community,
abandoning the root and grasping at the branch,
not seeking the origin.
They drift in the five paths
and are unable to free themselves.
Therefore, practitioners should diligently uphold the precept against killing.
For example, there is a person
who grinds a large stone
with diligent effort,
spending days and months
to make a small toy ox.
The effort is heavy,
but the result is very light.
People in the world are also like this.
Grinding the large stone is analogous to studying and learning
with diligent labor, while making a small ox is analogous to fame and mutual quarrels.
As for those who study, they should deeply contemplate, extensively learn, and widely understand.
They should practice accordingly and seek superior fruits far away.
Instead, they seek fame
with arrogance and pride,
increasing faults and harms.
For example, there is a person
who, because of hunger,
eats seven fried cakes.
After eating six and a half cakes,
he becomes full.
The person becomes angry and regretful,
hitting himself with his hand
and saying:
"I am now full
because of this half-cake.
The previous six cakes were wasted in vain.
If I had known that half a cake could be enough,
I should have eaten it first."
People in the world are also like this.
From the beginning, they have always lacked happiness.
Yet, in their delusion,
they create the idea of happiness.
Like that foolish person
who thought that half a cake made him full,
worldly people are ignorant
and regard wealth and honor as happiness.
As for wealth and honor, it is very bitter when seeking them,
and once obtained,
it is also bitter to protect them.
When they are lost later,
worry and anxiety are again bitter.
In these three times, there is no happiness at all.
It is like clothing and food
that are called happiness because they provide cover,
and in hardship, they falsely create the idea of happiness.
The Buddhas say:
"The three realms are without peace;
all are great suffering.
Ordinary people are deluded
and falsely create the idea of happiness."
For example, there is a person
who is about to travel far away
and commands his servant:
"You should guard the door well
and watch the donkey rope."
After his master leaves,
at that time, the neighbors have music and entertainment.
This servant wants to listen
but cannot settle himself.
He then ties the door with the rope
and places it on the donkey,
carrying it to the place of entertainment
to listen to the music.
After the servant leaves,
the thieves take away all the property in the house.
The master returns home
and asks his servant:
"Where are the treasures?"
The servant then replies:
"Master, you first entrusted the door, the donkey, and the rope to me.
Other than that, I know nothing."
The master further says:
"I left you to guard the door precisely for the sake of the property.
Now that the property is lost,
what is the use of the door?"
Foolish people in the cycle of birth and death, like servants of love, are also like this.
The Tathāgata's teachings
constantly protect the root faculties
and do not cling to the six dusts,
guarding the donkey of ignorance
and watching the rope of love.
But these *bǐqiū* do not follow the Buddha's teachings.
They greedily seek profit and offerings
and falsely appear pure and sit in quiet places,
their minds flowing and chasing,
greedily clinging to the five desires,
being confused and disordered by sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures.
Ignorance covers their minds,
and the rope of love binds them.
Right mindfulness, the factors of enlightenment, and the treasures of the path are all scattered and lost.
For example, a village jointly steals a yak and eats it together.
The one who lost the yak follows the tracks to the village,
calls out to the villagers,
and asks them about the situation,
saying to them:
"You are in this village."
The one who did not steal replies:
"I have no village."
He is further asked:
"In your village, there is a pond.
Did you eat the yak together by this pond?"
He replies: "There is no pond."
He is further asked:
"Is there a tree by the pond?"
He replies: "There is no tree."
He is further asked:
"When you stole the yak, was it east of your village?"
He replies: "There is no east."
He is further asked:
"When you stole the yak, was it not at midday?"
He replies: "There is no midday."
He is further asked:
"Even if there is no village and no tree,
how can there be no east and no time under the heavens?
Knowing that you are lying and cannot be trusted at all,
did you steal and eat the yak?"
He replies:
"Indeed, we ate it."
Those who break the precepts are also like this.
They cover up their faults
and are unwilling to confess them.
When they die and enter hell,
the devas and benevolent gods, with their divine eyes, observe
and cannot be deceived,
like that eating of the yak
that could not be denied.
In the past, on the day of the *jié fǎ qìng* festival in a foreign country, all the women held *yōubōluó huā* lotuses as garlands and ornaments.
There was a poor man whose
wife said to him:
"If you can get *yōubōluó huā* lotuses
and bring them to me,
I will be your wife;
if you cannot get them,
I will leave you."
Her husband had always been good at making the sound of mandarin ducks.
He then entered the king's pond
and made the sound of mandarin ducks
to steal *yōubōluó huā* lotuses.
The guard of the pond then asked:
"Who is in the pond?"
This poor man inadvertently replied:
"I am a mandarin duck."
The guard caught him
and took him to the king.
On the way, he again made the sound
of mandarin ducks,
and the guard of the pond said:
"You didn't do it before;
what is the use of doing it now?"
Foolish people in the world are also like this.
Throughout their lives, they harm
and create many evil deeds,
not practicing the mind
to make it disciplined and good.
When approaching the end of their lives,
they say: "Now I want to cultivate goodness."
The prison guards take them away and hand them over to King *Yánluó*,
and even if they want to cultivate goodness,
it is too late.
Like that foolish person
who wanted to go to the king's place
and make the sound of mandarin ducks.
For example, a jackal is under a tree.
The wind blows and breaks a branch
that falls on its back.
It immediately closes its eyes
and does not want to look at the tree.
It abandons it and runs away
to an open space,
and even until sunset,
it does not dare to come back.
From afar, it sees the branches of a large tree moving up and down in the wind
and thinks it is calling him.
He then comes under the tree.
Foolish disciples are also like this.
Having already left home
and being able to be near their teachers,
they run away even with a small reprimand.
Later, they encounter evil friends
who constantly harass and disturb them.
Then they return to where
they left. Such going and coming is foolish and deluded.
For example, in the past, two children entered a river to play.
At the bottom of the water, they found a handful of hair.
One child said:
"This is a fairy's beard."
The other child said:
"This is bear fur."
At that time, there was a hermit by the river.
These two children argued endlessly.
They went to the hermit's place
to resolve their doubts.
The hermit immediately took rice and sesame seeds,
chewed them in his mouth,
and spat them into his palm.
He said to the children:
"What is in my palm looks like peacock droppings."
But this hermit did not answer their question;
everyone knew it.
The foolish people of the world are also like this;
when preaching the Dharma, they speak frivolously about various Dharmas
and do not answer the true principles.
Like that hermit who did not answer the question,
they are ridiculed by everyone.
Superficial and empty talk is also like this.
For example, someone
suddenly suffers from kyphosis
and asks a doctor to treat it.
The doctor applies ghee,
places boards above and below,
and presses hard,
unknowingly causing both eyes to pop out at once.
The foolish people of the world are also like this;
for the sake of cultivating blessings,
they engage in business and trade
and commit various illegal acts.
Although the matter is successful,
the profit does not make up for the harm;
in the future, they will enter hell, like the eyes popping out.
For example, five people jointly buy a maid.
One of them tells the maid:
"Wash my clothes."
Then another person also tells her to wash clothes.
The maid says to the second person:
"I'll wash his first."
The latter angrily says:
"I bought you together with the first person,
why only him?"
He then whips her ten times;
each of the five people whips her ten times.
The five *yīns* are also like this;
afflictions cause the formation of this body.
These five *yīns* constantly scourge sentient beings with birth, old age, sickness, death, and limitless suffering.
For example, a performer
performs music before the king.
The king promises a thousand coins.
Later, he asks the king for them,
but the king does not give them.
The king tells him:
"You performed music earlier,
which only pleased my ears;
my giving you money
would only please your ears."
The fruits of karma in the world are also like this;
although one may receive a little happiness in the human or heavenly realms,
it is not real.
Impermanent, decaying, and not lasting long,
like that empty music.
For example, a teacher has two disciples.
The teacher suffers from a leg ailment.
He tells the two disciples to massage one leg each in turn.
The two disciples constantly hate and are jealous of each other.
One disciple is massaging,
and the other disciple grabs the leg that he should be massaging and breaks it with a stone.
When the first disciple comes,
he is angry at this
and grabs the leg that the other person was massaging and breaks it as well.
Students of the Buddha-dharma are also like this;
those who study *fāngděng* (Mahayana) criticize the *xiǎochéng* (Hinayana),
and those who study *xiǎochéng* (Hinayana) criticize the *fāngděng* (Mahayana),
thus causing the Great Sage's teachings to perish on both paths.
For example, there is a snake.
The tail says to the head:
"I should be in front."
The head says to the tail:
"I am always in front,
why suddenly?"
The head is indeed in front,
but the tail wraps around a tree
and cannot move forward.
Letting the tail be in front,
it immediately falls into a fire pit
and is burned to death.
Teachers and disciples are also like this;
they say the teacher is old
and should always be in front,
but the young should be the leaders.
Such young people are not familiar with the precepts
and commit many offenses,
thus dragging each other into hell.
Once, there was a king
who had a trusted retainer.
In the midst of battle, the retainer risked his life to save the king, ensuring his safety.
The king was very happy
and granted him whatever he wished.
He immediately asked:
"What do you seek?
Whatever you desire."
The retainer replied:
"When the king shaves his beard, I wish to be the one to shave it."
The king said:
"If this pleases you,
I grant you your wish."
Such a foolish person is laughed at by the world;
the rule of half the kingdom, the assistance of high ministers, all could have been obtained,
but he seeks a lowly occupation.
Foolish people are also like this;
the Buddhas, through countless eons, achieved Buddhahood through difficult practices.
If one encounters a Buddha or comes across his teachings, a human body is difficult to obtain,
like a blind turtle encountering a floating wooden hole.
These two are difficult to encounter;
now we have encountered them,
but our minds are inferior.
Holding a few precepts, they think it is enough,
and do not seek the supreme Dharma of *nièpán* (nirvana).
Without the intention to advance and seek,
they engage in wrongdoings
and think it is enough.
Once there were two people
traveling together on the road
who saw a person with a sesame cart on a dangerous road
unable to move forward.
The person with the cart said to the two people:
"Help me push the cart out of this dangerous road."
The two people replied:
"What will you give us?"
The person with the cart said:
"I have nothing to give you."
The two people then helped push the cart
to flat ground
and said to the person with the cart:
"Give us something."
He replied: "Nothing."
Again they said:
"Give us nothing."
Among the two people, one smiled and said:
"He is unwilling to give, why be sad?"
The other person replied:
"Giving me 'nothing'
must involve having 'nothing'."
The first person said:
"The two characters 'nothing' combined
are a false name."
Ordinary worldly people, if there is nothing,
then give rise to a realm of no-thing.
The second person said,
"Nothing" is precisely no-sign, no-vow, no-action.
Once there was a wealthy elder;
those around him, wanting to please him,
were all extremely respectful.
When the elder spat,
the attendants around him stepped on it to cover it.
There was a foolish person who could not get to it in time
and said:
"If he spits on the ground,
everyone steps on it to cover it.
When he is about to spit,
I should step on it first."
Then, the elder was just about to cough and spit,
and this foolish person immediately raised his foot and stepped on the elder's mouth,
breaking his lip and teeth.
The elder said to the foolish person:
"Why did you step on my lip and mouth?"
The foolish person replied:
"If the elder's saliva comes out of his mouth and falls to the ground,
the flattering attendants have already stepped on it,
and I can never get to it in time.
For this reason, when the saliva is about to come out, I raise my foot and step on it first,
hoping to please you."
Everything needs its time;
when the time has not yet arrived,
forcibly applying effort
leads to suffering.
For this reason,
people in the world should know about timing and non-timing.
Once, in the *Móluó* (Malla) kingdom, there was a *chàlì* (Kshatriya)
who became seriously ill.
Knowing that he would definitely die,
he instructed his two sons:
"After I die, divide the wealth well."
The two sons followed his instructions.
After his death, they divided it into two parts.
The elder brother said
that the younger brother's share was not equal.
At that time, there was a foolish old man who said:
"I will teach you how to divide the things
so that it is equal.
Break all the existing things into two parts.
How to break them?
Cut the clothes in the middle into two parts;
break the plates and bottles in the middle into two parts;
break all the earthenware pots and jars into two parts;
break the coins into two parts.
Thus, all the property should be broken into two parts."
Such a way of dividing things is ridiculed by people.
Like the various heretical paths
exclusively cultivate differentialist theories,
the doors to these theories have four kinds:
There is the door of definitive answers,
for example, all people without exception must die,
this is the door of definitive answers.
That those who die must be born
is an answer requiring differentiation,
those whose love is exhausted have no birth,
those with love must have birth,
this is called the door of answers requiring differentiation.
Someone asks, are humans the most superior?
One should ask in return:
"Are you asking about the three evil paths?
Or are you asking about the various heavens?
If you ask about the three evil paths,
humans are indeed the most superior;
if you ask about the various heavens,
humans are certainly inferior."
Such meanings are called the door of counter-questioning answers.
If asked about the fourteen unanswerables,
if asked whether the world and sentient beings are finite or infinite, have a beginning and end or no beginning and end,
such meanings are called the door of unanswered responses.
The heretics are foolish
yet consider themselves wise,
refuting the four kinds of theories
and making one differentialist theory,
like a foolish person dividing money,
breaking the coins into two pieces.
For example, two people go to a potter's place,
watching him tread the wheel and make clay pots,
watching without weariness.
One person leaves,
going to a great assembly,
obtaining excellent food
and also acquiring precious jewels;
the other person watches the pot
and says this:
"I'll wait until I finish watching."
In this way, gradually until sunset,
continuing to watch the pot
and losing food and clothing.
Foolish people are also like this,
repairing household affairs
without realizing impermanence.
Today managing this affair,
tomorrow creating that task,
the Buddhas, great dragons, appear,
the thunderous sound pervades the world,
the rain of Dharma is without obstruction,
but due to entangled affairs, they do not hear.
Not knowing that the messenger of death arrives,
they miss this assembly of Buddhas,
not obtaining the precious jewels of the Dharma,
constantly dwelling in the poverty of evil paths.
Turning their backs and abandoning the true Dharma,
they watch the pot of entangled affairs,
ultimately without end or conclusion,
therefore losing the benefit of the Dharma,
never having a time of liberation."
Once there was a foolish person
who went to a large pond,
seeing in the water's reflection a true golden image,
thinking there was gold,
he immediately entered the water
and stirred up the mud, seeking it.
Exhausted and unable to find it,
he came out and sat down again.
After a short while, the water cleared
and the golden color appeared again,
he again entered inside
and stirred up the mud, seeking it even more,
but also could not find it.
Just like this, his father looked for his son,
found him, and asked his son,
"What are you doing,
so tired?"
The son said to his father,
"There is true gold at the bottom of the water,
I then threw myself into the water
wanting to stir up the mud to take it,
but I am exhausted and cannot find it."
The father looked at the true gold's shadow at the bottom of the water,
and knew this gold was on a tree,
the reason he knew was that the shadow appeared at the bottom of the water.
His father said,
"Certainly a flying bird carried the gold and put it on the tree."
Immediately following his father's words, he climbed the tree and found it.
Ordinary foolish people,
without wisdom, are also like this,
in the non-self aggregates,
they wrongly generate the thought of self;
like seeing the golden shadow,
diligently and painfully seeking,
futile labor without attainment."
The crowd of Brāhmaṇas all said:
"Great Brahman is the father of the world,
able to create all things."
A disciple of the creator of all things said,
"I can also create all things,"
truly foolish
considering himself wise.
He said to Brahman:
"I want to create all things."
King Brahman said:
"Do not make this intention,
you cannot create."
Not using the deva's words,
he then wanted to create things.
Brahman saw the things his disciple created,
and said to him:
"You made the head too big,
made the neck extremely small,
made the hands too big,
made the arms extremely small,
made the feet extremely small,
made the heels extremely big,
made it look like a *pīśāca* ghost."
From this meaning, one should know, each is created by their own karma, not created by Brahman,
the Buddhas teach the Dharma without clinging to two extremes,
not clinging to annihilation
nor clinging to permanence,
like teaching the Dharma of the Eightfold Path.
The heretics, seeing
the affairs of annihilation and permanence,
then generate attachment,
deceiving the world
creating Dharma images,
what is said is truly non-Dharma.
Once there was a person
sick and seriously ill,
a good doctor diagnosed him, saying:
"He must constantly eat one kind of pheasant meat
to be able to recover from the illness."
This patient then bought a pheasant from the market,
ate it all,
and never ate it again.
The doctor saw him later and asked him:
"Has your illness recovered yet?"
The patient answered,
"The doctor first taught me to constantly eat pheasant meat,
therefore now I have eaten one pheasant completely and dare not eat it again."
The doctor again said:
"If the previous pheasant is already finished, why not eat more?
How do you now expect to be cured by just eating one pheasant?"
All the heretics are also like this,
hearing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, unsurpassed good doctors, say,
one should understand consciousness,
the heretics cling to the view of permanence,
then they say that past, future, and present are only one consciousness
without change,
like eating one pheasant,
therefore unable to cure the illness of their ignorance and afflictions.
The wise Buddhas teach the heretics to remove their view of permanence,
all dharmas are produced and extinguished moment by moment,
how can there be one consciousness that is constant and unchanging?
Like the worldly doctor teaching to eat more pheasant to recover from the illness,
the Buddha is also like this,
teaching all sentient beings
to understand
that because all dharmas are destroyed, they are not permanent, and because they continue, they are not annihilated,
and then they can eradicate the illness of the view of permanence.
Once, in the country of *Gāndhāra*, there were many performers,
due to famine and scarcity, they sought food in other lands,
passing through *Pólúoxīn* Mountain,
and in this mountain there were always many evil ghosts, *rākṣasas* who eat people.
At that time, the various performers gathered to stay overnight in the mountain,
the wind and cold in the mountain,
they lit a fire and slept,
among the performers, there was one who was suffering from the cold,
wearing the theatrical costume of a *rākṣasa*,
sitting towards the fire.
At that time, among the companions, those who woke up from sleep, suddenly saw a *rākṣasa* by the fire,
without carefully observing,
abandoned him and ran,
then startling and agitating each other,
all the companions fled and ran away.
At that time, the one among the companions wearing the *rākṣasa* costume, also followed and chased after them,
running away in haste,
the other companions, seeing him behind,
thought he wanted to harm them,
doubling their fear and panic,
crossing mountains and rivers,
throwing themselves into ditches and ravines,
their bodies injured and broken,
exhausted and collapsing,
until dawn
they realized it was not a ghost.
All ordinary people are also like this,
dwelling in the famine of afflictions and scarcity of good dharmas,
and wanting to seek afar the unsurpassed food of Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
then within the five aggregates, they wrongly calculate a self.
Due to the view of self, they flow and rush in saṃsāra,
chased by afflictions, unable to be at ease,
falling into the ravines of the three evil paths,
until dawn, symbolizing the end of the night of saṃsāra,
with the wisdom of understanding, they then know that there is no true self in the five aggregates.
Once upon a time, there was an old house.
People said that this house was always haunted by evil ghosts,
and everyone was afraid
and dared not sleep there.
At that time, there was a man
who claimed to be very brave
and said:
"I want to enter this house
and stay for a night."
So he went in and stayed.
Later, there was another person
who claimed to be even braver than the first man.
He heard from the people around that there were always evil ghosts in this house,
so he wanted to enter
and pushed the door forward.
The man who had entered earlier thought he was a ghost
and pushed the door back to prevent him from entering.
The man who came later also thought there was a ghost,
and the two men fought.
It went on until dawn. When they saw each other, they realized that neither was a ghost.
All people in the world are also like this.
Causes and conditions temporarily come together without a master.
When analyzed one by one, who is the self?
However, all sentient beings arbitrarily judge right and wrong
and forcefully create disputes,
just like those two men, without any difference.
Once upon a time, there was a woman
who was extremely dissolute and licentious.
Her desire was so strong
that she hated her husband.
She constantly thought of ways
to plot to harm him.
She devised various schemes
but could not find a convenient opportunity.
It happened that her husband was hired to travel to a neighboring country as an envoy.
The woman secretly made a plan
to create poisonous pills
to harm her husband.
She deceitfully said to her husband:
"Now you are going on a long journey,
and I am worried you may lack supplies.
So I have made five hundred *huānxǐ* pills
to use as provisions
to send to you.
If you leave the country and reach another territory,
you can take and eat them when you are hungry and tired."
The husband followed her words.
After arriving in another territory,
before he had a chance to eat them,
he stopped for the night in a forest in the dark.
Fearing wild beasts,
he climbed a tree to avoid them.
He forgot to put the *huānxǐ* pills under the tree.
That very night, five hundred thieves
stole five hundred horses and treasures from the king of that country
and stopped under the tree.
Because they were fleeing in haste,
they were all hungry and thirsty.
They saw the *huānxǐ* pills under the tree.
The thieves took them
and each ate one pill.
The poison's potency was strong.
All five hundred thieves died at the same time.
The man in the tree until dawn,
saw this group of thieves dead under the tree.
He pretended to slash and shoot the corpses with knives and arrows.
He collected their saddles, horses, and treasures
and drove them towards that country.
At that time, the king of that country led many people
to follow the tracks.
They met the man on the road.
The king asked him:
"Who are you?
Where did you get these horses?"
The man replied:
"I am a person from a certain country.
On the road, I encountered this group of thieves
who were slashing and shooting at each other.
All five hundred thieves are now dead in one place under a tree.
Because of this, I obtained these horses and treasures
and came to submit to your kingdom.
If you don't believe me,
you can send someone to see the wounds and the place of the massacre."
The king then sent a trusted aide to investigate
and it was just as he had said.
The king was delighted
and marveled at this unprecedented event.
After returning to the country,
he bestowed great honors and rewards,
generously gave him treasures,
and enfeoffed him with a village.
The old officials of that king all became jealous and said to the king:
"He is a foreigner
and cannot be fully trusted.
How can you suddenly favor him so greatly,
bestowing honors and rewards
that surpass the old officials?"
The foreigner heard this and said:
"Who is brave and strong enough to compete with me?
I invite them to demonstrate their skills on the plains."
The old officials were stunned and no one dared to challenge him.
Later, in the great wilderness of that country, there was a fierce lion
that blocked the road, killing people
and cutting off the king's road.
At that time, the old officials discussed it in detail:
"That foreigner claims to be brave and strong and that no one can defeat him.
Now, if he can kill that lion and eliminate the harm for the country,
it would truly be extraordinary."
After making this decision, they reported it to the king. The king, after hearing this,
gave him a sword and staff and immediately sent him off.
At that time, the foreigner, after receiving the order,
strengthened his resolve
and headed towards the lion's location.
The lion saw him,
became agitated, roared, leaped, and moved forward.
The foreigner was frightened
and immediately climbed a tree.
The lion opened its mouth
and looked up at the tree.
The man, in his fear and panic,
lost his grip on the knife,
and it fell into the lion's mouth.
The lion immediately died.
At that time, the foreigner rejoiced and leaped with joy.
He came to report to the king.
The king doubled his favor and rewards.
At that time, the people of that country readily respected and admired him
and all praised him.
The woman's *huānxǐ* pills are a metaphor for impure giving.
The king's envoy is a metaphor for a good teacher.
Going to another country is a metaphor for going to the heavens.
Killing the thieves is a metaphor for attaining *xūtuóhuán* and forcefully cutting off the five desires and all afflictions.
Meeting the king of that country is a metaphor for encountering sages.
The old people of the country who became jealous are a metaphor for the heretics who, when they see wise people who can cut off afflictions and the five desires,
then slander them, saying that there is no such thing.
The foreigner who vigorously declares that the old officials are not capable of competing with him is a metaphor for those heretics who dare not resist.
Killing the lion is a metaphor for destroying demons.
Having cut off afflictions and subdued evil demons,
one then attains the unattached fruit of the path and receives rewards.
Being constantly fearful and apprehensive is a metaphor for being able to use weakness to control strength.
Although in the beginning there was no pure intention,
nevertheless, that giving, upon encountering a good teacher,
then obtains a superior reward.
Impure giving is still like this,
how much more so is giving with a good and joyful heart?
Therefore, one should diligently cultivate giving in the field of blessings.

Once upon a time, there was the son of a wealthy man
who entered the sea with merchants to collect treasures.
This son of a wealthy man was skilled in reciting the methods of entering the sea and steering a boat.
If entering seawater vortexes, eddies, and places of reefs and rapids,
one should steer like this,
correct like this,
remain like this.
He said to the people:
"I know all the methods of entering the sea."
Having heard this, the crowd deeply believed his words.
Once they arrived in the sea,
before much time had passed, the ship's master fell ill
and suddenly died.
At that time, the son of the elder immediately took his place.
Arriving at the swirling, swift currents,
he shouted,
"You must grasp it like this! Correct it like this!"
The boat spun around and around,
unable to move forward towards the treasure.
All the merchants on the boat drowned.
Ordinary people are also like this:
they briefly study Chan practice, Ānpān breath counting, and the Contemplation of Impurity;
although they recite the words, they do not understand their meaning;
they do not comprehend the various methods
but declare themselves to be knowledgeable,
falsely transmitting the Chan Dharma,
causing those before them to become confused and lose their minds, distorting the characteristics of the Dharma.
Year after year, they gain nothing,
like that foolish person who caused others to drown in the sea.
Once, there was a married couple
with three *bǐng* cakes.
The couple divided them,
each eating one cake.
One *bǐng* remained.
Together, they made an agreement:
"Whoever speaks will not get the cake."
Having made the agreement,
for the sake of the one *bǐng*, neither dared to speak.
After a while, a thief
entered the house to steal,
taking their belongings.
Everything they had was taken by the thief's hand;
the couple, because of their prior agreement, watched without speaking.
Seeing that they did not speak,
the thief violated the wife in front of her husband.
The husband saw this but still did not speak.
The wife then called out to the thief,
and said to her husband,
"Why are you such a fool? For the sake of one *bǐng*, you see the thief but don't call out?"
Her husband clapped his hands and laughed, saying,
"Hey, woman!
I'm definitely getting the *bǐng*;
I won't share it with you anymore!"
When people heard this, they all laughed and ridiculed him.
Ordinary people are also like this:
for the sake of small fame and profit, they falsely appear calm and silent.
They are invaded by the various evil thieves of false afflictions.
Losing their good Dharma,
they fall into the three evil paths,
without any fear
of seeking a way to escape the world.
They indulge in the five desires,
becoming addicted to play and amusement.
Although they encounter great suffering,
they do not consider it a problem,
just like those foolish people, there is no difference.
Once, there was a person
who was angry with someone else,
and was sad and unhappy.
Someone asked him,
"Why are you so distressed like this now?"
He immediately replied,
"Someone has slandered me,
and I am unable to retaliate.
I don't know how to get revenge,
that's why I'm sad."
Someone said,
"Only the *Pítóluó* mantra can harm him,
but there is one problem:
before harming him, it will harm you instead."
After hearing this, the person was very happy.
"Please just teach me!
Even if I am harmed, I hope to injure him."
The people of the world are also like this:
for the sake of anger, they want to seek the *Pítóluó* mantra,
to trouble the other person.
In the end, without harming others,
they are first harmed by their own anger,
falling into hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts,
just like those foolish people, there is no difference.
Once, there was a person
who traveled from Northern *Tiānzhú* to Southern *Tiānzhú*.
After staying there for a long time, he married a local woman.
At that time, the wife prepared food for her husband,
and the husband hastily swallowed it
without avoiding the heat.
The wife then found it strange
and said to her husband,
"There are no robbers here who seize people.
What is the urgent matter
that you are in such a hurry?
Why don't you eat slowly?"
The husband replied to his wife,
"There is a good secret
that I cannot tell you."
Hearing his words,
the wife thought there was some special method,
and earnestly asked him about it.
After a long time, he finally answered,
"Since my ancestors,
the family tradition has been to eat quickly.
I am now imitating them,
that is why I am fast."
Ordinary people in the world are also like this:
not understanding correct principles,
not knowing good from evil,
they commit various evil deeds
without shame,
and say,
"Since my ancestors, we have practiced this way."
Until death, they follow this practice
and never abandon it,
like that foolish person who practiced quick eating as a good method.
Once, there was an elder
who sent someone with money to another garden
to buy *ānpóluó* fruit
to eat,
and instructed him,
"You should buy the sweetest and most delicious ones."
He immediately took the money and went to buy the fruit.
The fruit seller said,
"All the fruits on this tree are good and delicious;
there are no bad ones.
If you taste one fruit,
it will be enough to know."
The buyer said,
"I will taste each one
and then buy them.
If I only taste one,
how can I know?"
He then took the fruits
and tasted each one,
bringing them back home.
The elder saw them
and disliked them, not eating them,
throwing them all away.
People in the world are also like this:
hearing that upholding the precepts and giving alms brings great wealth and happiness,
and that the body is always peaceful and free from illness,
they do not believe it.
They then say,
"If giving alms brings blessings,
I will only believe it when I get them myself."
They see with their own eyes that the noble and the lowly, the rich and the poor in this world are all the results of past karma,
but they do not know how to infer cause and effect from one example.
They harbor disbelief,
waiting to experience it themselves.
Once their life ends,
their wealth is lost,
like tasting the fruit
and throwing it all away.
Once there was a person
who married two wives.
If he was intimate with one, he would be resented by the other.
Unable to resolve this,
he laid down straight on his back between the two wives.
It happened to rain heavily,
and the house leaked.
Water and mud fell together,
landing in his eyes.
Because of his prior agreement
not to move, he did not dare to get up and avoid it,
causing both his eyes to lose their sight.
Ordinary people in the world are also like this:
associating with evil friends
and practicing unlawful deeds,
creating karma
and falling into the three evil paths,
remaining in the cycle of birth and death for a long time,
losing the eye of wisdom,
like that foolish man
who lost both his eyes for the sake of his two wives.
Once, there was a person
who went to his wife's house,
and saw her pounding rice.
He went to her side
and stole rice to put in his mouth.
The wife came to her husband
wanting to talk to him,
but his mouth was full of rice
and he couldn't respond.
Ashamed in front of his wife,
he refused to spit it out,
so he didn't speak.
The wife was surprised that he didn't speak,
and touched his mouth,
thinking it was swollen.
She told her father,
"My husband suddenly
got a mouth swelling,
and can't speak at all."
Her father then called a doctor to treat him.
The doctor said,
"This disease is very serious;
it can only be cured
by cutting it open with a knife."
Even if one uses a knife to cut open the mouth,
and the rice comes out from within,
the matter is revealed.
The people of the world are also like this;
committing all kinds of evil deeds,
violating pure precepts,
covering up their transgressions,
unwilling to disclose them,
they fall into the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts.
Like that foolish person
who, for the sake of a little shame, was unwilling to spit out the rice,
having his mouth cut open with a knife,
his transgression was then revealed.
In the past, there was a person
who rode a black horse
into battle to strike the thieves.
Because of his fear, he could not fight,
so he smeared blood on his face
and pretended to be dead,
lying among the dead people.
The horse he was riding was seized by others.
After the army had left,
he wanted to return home,
so he cut off the tail of another person's white horse
and brought it back.
After he arrived home,
someone asked him,
"Where is the horse you were riding now?
Why aren't you riding it?"
He replied,
"My horse is already dead,
so I brought the tail."
The person beside him said,
"Your horse was originally black;
why is the tail white?"
He was silent and had nothing to say,
and was laughed at by people.
The people of the world are also like this,
saying of themselves that they are good and virtuous,
cultivating loving-kindness,
and not eating wine or meat,
yet they kill living beings
and inflict all kinds of cruel punishments.
They falsely claim to be good
and leave no evil undone,
like that foolish person
who falsely said his horse was dead.
In the past, there was a king
who established teachings and laws.
All the *Bāluómén* and others in my kingdom must observe purification;
those who do not observe purification will be driven to be whipped and made to do all kinds of hard labor.
There was a *Bāluómén* who held an empty bathing vessel,
pretending to be purified.
When people poured water on him,
he immediately poured it away.
Then he said,
"I am not being purified;
the king himself is purifying me."
Because of the king's intention, he avoided the king's labor,
falsely claiming purification
but not actually purifying himself.
Ordinary householders who have left home are also like this;
shaving their heads and wearing robes,
but inwardly violating the precepts.
They falsely appear to uphold the precepts,
hoping to seek profit and offerings and also to avoid the king's labor.
Outwardly they seem like *Shāmén*,
but inwardly they are false and deceitful,
like holding an empty bottle,
only having an external appearance.
In the past, there was a person
who first filled a jar with grain.
A camel put its head into the jar to eat the grain
but then could not get out,
and being unable to get out, it was worried and distressed.
An old man came and said to him,
"Do not worry!
I will teach you how to get it out.
If you use my words,
you will surely get it out quickly.
You should cut off its head,
and then it will come out by itself."
He immediately used his words
and cut off the camel's head with a knife,
thus both killing the camel and breaking the jar.
Such a foolish person is laughed at by the world.
Ordinary foolish people are also like this,
hoping for *Pútí*
and aspiring to the Three Vehicles.
They should uphold the precepts
and guard against all evils,
but for the sake of the five desires, they destroy their pure precepts.
Having violated the precepts, they abandon the Three Vehicles,
letting their minds run wild and doing every evil.
Both the Vehicle and the pure precepts are discarded,
like that foolish person who lost both the camel and the jar.
In the past, there was a farmer
who traveled to the cities
and saw the king's daughter.
Her countenance was upright and beautiful,
something rarely seen.
He thought of her day and night,
and his feelings could not stop.
He thought of having intercourse with her
but there was no way to fulfill it.
His complexion turned sallow
and he became seriously ill.
All those who were close to him asked him, "Why are you like this?"
He replied to his relatives,
"Yesterday I saw the king's daughter,
her countenance was upright and beautiful,
and I thought of having intercourse with her,
but because I could not obtain it, I am sick.
If I cannot get her,
I will surely die."
The relatives said,
"We will make good arrangements for you
to enable you to obtain her;
do not be sad."
The next day they saw him
and said to him,
"We have made arrangements for you and it has been obtained,
only the king's daughter is unwilling."
The farmer heard this
and smiled with joy,
thinking he would surely obtain her.
The foolish people of the world are also like this,
not distinguishing the seasons, spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
they throw seeds into the soil in winter
hoping to obtain fruit.
They waste their efforts in vain
and obtain nothing,
the sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves are all lost.
Foolish people in the world cultivate little blessings
and think they are complete.
They then think that *Pútí* can be attained,
like that farmer hoping for the king's daughter.
In the past, people from the border country did not recognize donkeys.
They heard someone say that donkey milk is very good,
but no one recognized a donkey.
At that time, the people obtained a male donkey
and wanted to milk it.
They fought to grab it.
Among them, some grabbed the head,
some grabbed the ears,
some grabbed the tail,
and some grabbed the feet.
There were also those who grabbed the container,
each wanting to be the first to obtain it
and drink it in front.
Someone grabbed the donkey's penis
thinking it was milk,
and immediately milked it,
hoping to obtain the milk.
The people were tired and weary
and obtained nothing.
They labored in vain
and gained nothing,
and were ridiculed by all the people of the world.
Non-Buddhist outsiders are also like this,
hearing about the *Dào*
but not seeking the right place.
They give rise to false thoughts,
generating all kinds of wrong views.
They go naked, starve themselves,
throw themselves off cliffs, and rush into fire.
Because of these wrong views, they fall into evil paths,
like those foolish people falsely seeking milk.
In the past, there was a person
who spoke to his child at night, saying,
"Tomorrow I will go with you to that village
to ask for something."
After the child heard this,
the next morning,
without even asking his father,
he went alone to that place.
Having arrived there,
his body was exhausted
and he obtained nothing.
Furthermore, he did not get food
and was dying of hunger and thirst.
He then returned
and saw his father.
When the father saw his son coming back,
he severely rebuked him, saying,
"You are very foolish
and have no wisdom.
Why didn't you wait for me?
You went back and forth in vain,
suffering hardships for nothing,
and are ridiculed by all the people of the world."
Ordinary people are also like this.
Even if they become monks,
shave their heads,
and wear the three robes,
they do not seek out wise teachers
to consult and receive the Dharma.
They lose all their *chán dìng*
and the merits of the *dào pǐn*, and all the wonderful fruits of a *shā mén* are lost.
Like that foolish man,
they vainly go back and forth,
only tiring themselves.
They appear to be *shā mén*,
but in reality, they gain nothing.
Once there was a king
who wanted to enter the Garden of No Sorrow
to enjoy himself.
He ordered a minister, saying:
"Take a stool
and carry it to that garden
so that I may sit and rest."
At that time, that messenger was ashamed and unwilling to take it.
He said to the king:
"I cannot take it;
I wish to carry it."
Then the king placed thirty-six stools on his back
and drove him to carry them to the garden.
Such a foolish man is laughed at by the world.
Ordinary people are also like this.
If they see a single hair of a woman on the ground,
they claim to uphold the precepts
and refuse to pick it up.
Later, they are deluded by afflictions,
and do not consider the thirty-six impure substances—hair, nails, teeth, excrement, and urine—to be repulsive.
They grasp all thirty-six substances at once
without shame,
and do not relinquish them until death,
like that foolish man carrying the stools.
Once there was a man
suffering from a disease in his lower body.
The doctor said:
"It must be treated with an enema to be cured."
He gathered the equipment for the enema
intending to administer it.
Before the doctor arrived,
he took it orally,
his abdomen swelled, and he was near death
unable to control himself.
The doctor arrived
and was surprised by what had happened.
He immediately asked:
"Why is it like this?"

He replied to the doctor, "Earlier, I took the enema medicine orally, so I am near death." Hearing this, the doctor deeply rebuked him, saying, "You are a great fool who does not understand the expedient means." Then he gave him the remaining medicine orally to induce vomiting and purging, and he was cured. Such a foolish man is laughed at by the world.
Ordinary people are also like this.
Wanting to cultivate *chán*
and study various methods,
they should emulate the contemplation of impurity,
but instead emulate counting breaths;
those who should count breaths
emulate contemplation of the six realms.
They reverse the order
without any foundation,
vainly wasting their lives
and being troubled by it.
Without consulting a good teacher,
they invert the *chán* methods,
like that foolish man drinking impure substances.
Once there were a father and son
traveling with companions.
The son entered a forest
and was bitten by a bear.
His claws damaged his body.
In distress, he left the forest
and returned to his companions.
The father saw that his son's body was injured
and asked in surprise:
"Why are you harmed by these wounds?"
The son reported to his father:
"There was a kind of creature
with shaggy
hair that came and harmed me."
The father took up his bow and arrow
and went to the forest.
He saw a hermit
with long hair
and wanted to shoot him.
Someone nearby said:
"Why shoot him?
This man is harmless;
you should punish the one who is guilty."
Foolish people in the world are also like this.
They abuse those who wear the robes but do not practice the *dào*,
and harm good and virtuous people,
like that father whose son was injured by a bear but wrongly accused a divine immortal.
Once there was a rustic man
who came to the fields
and saw good wheat seedlings
growing luxuriantly.
He asked the owner of the wheat:
"How can you make this wheat grow so well?"
The owner replied:
"By leveling the ground
and adding manure and water,
it grows like this."
That man immediately followed the method.
He mixed manure and water
and spread it on the field
and sowed the seeds on the ground.
Fearing that his own feet would tread on the ground, making it firm and preventing the wheat from growing,
he thought, "I will sit on a bed
and have people carry it
and scatter the seeds from above;
that will be good."
He had four men
each carrying one leg
to the field to scatter the seeds.
The ground became even harder,
and he was ridiculed by others.
Fearing his own two feet,
he added eight more feet.
Ordinary people are also like this.
Having cultivated the field of precepts
and good sprouts about to grow,
they should consult a teacher
and receive and practice the teachings
to allow the Dharma sprouts to grow.
Instead, they violate
and commit many evils,
causing the precept sprouts not to grow,
like that man
fearing his two feet
and adding eight more.
Once there was a monkey
beaten by an adult.
Unable to do anything about it,
it blamed a small child instead.
Ordinary foolish people are also like this.
The person who was angry before
has ceased to exist
and disappeared into the past,
but they mistake the subsequent arising Dharma as the former,
and falsely generate anger,
with hatred becoming deeper and deeper,
like that foolish monkey
beaten by an adult but blaming a small child instead.
Once, the *Āxiūluó* King saw the sun and moon shining brightly
and blocked them with his hand.
Ignorant common people wrongly punish dogs who are innocent.
Ordinary people are also like this.
They inflict suffering on their bodies
due to greed, anger, and ignorance,
lying on thorny beds
and scorching their bodies with five fires,
like eclipsing the moon
and wrongly beating the dog.
Once there was a woman
suffering greatly from eye pain.
A knowledgeable woman asked:
"Do your eyes hurt?"
She replied:
"My eyes hurt."
That woman then said:
"If you have eyes, you will surely have pain.
Although I have not yet had pain,
I want to pluck out my eyes
for fear of future pain."
Someone nearby said:
"If the eyes are there, they may or may not hurt,
but if the eyes are gone, there will be pain for the rest of your life."
Ordinary foolish people are also like this.
Hearing that wealth and high status are the root of decline and suffering,
they fear not giving alms
and fear future retribution,
even though their wealth is overflowing,
and suffer great distress.
Someone says:
"If you give alms, there may be suffering or happiness,
but if you do not give alms, there will be great suffering from poverty."
Like that woman,
unable to bear the immediate pain,
she wants to remove her eyes,
which would lead to long-term pain.
Once there were a father and son
traveling together on business.
Suddenly, robbers arose
wanting to strip them.
The son had a gold earring in his ear.
The father saw the robbers approaching,
fearing the loss of the earring,
and immediately pulled on it with his hand.
The ear did not immediately break,
and for the sake of the earring, he cut off his son's head.
In an instant, the robbers abandoned the attack and left.
He then put his son's head back on his shoulder
but it could not be fixed.
Such a foolish man is laughed at by the world.
Ordinary people are also like this.
For the sake of fame and gain, they create frivolous arguments.
They say that there is or is not a next life,
that there is or is not a *zhōngyīn* (intermediate state),
that mental phenomena exist or do not exist,
and they engage in various delusions, failing to grasp the truth of the Dharma.
When others refute their arguments with reasoned discourse,
they then say,
"My arguments never included such claims."
Such foolish people, for the sake of petty fame and gain, deliberately lie,
losing the fruits of the *shāmén* (ascetic) path.
When their bodies break down and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil paths,
like that foolish person
who, for the sake of a small gain, cut off his child's head.
Once upon a time, there was a group of thieves
who went out together to rob.
They took a lot of wealth
and divided it equally among themselves.
However, a *lùyě qīnbóluósè* (鹿野欽婆羅色) was not of pure quality,
so they considered it a lesser share
and gave it to the least of them.
The inferior one received it with resentment,
considering it a great loss.
He went to the city to sell it.
Many noble elders offered him a high price,
and the one man's gain was many times that of all his companions.
Only then was he joyous and immeasurably delighted.
It is like worldly people
who do not know whether there is retribution for giving,
but perform a small act of charity and are reborn in the heavens, enjoying immeasurable bliss.
Then they regret
not having given more extensively.
Like the *qīnbóluósè* (欽婆羅色)
that later fetched a great price, they then rejoice.
Giving is also like this:
doing a little and gaining much.
Only then do they congratulate themselves
and regret not having done more.
Once there was a monkey
holding a handful of beans.
It accidentally dropped one bean on the ground.
It then discarded the beans in its hand
to look for the one,
but before it found the one bean,
the chickens and ducks had eaten all the beans it had discarded.
Ordinary people who leave home are also like this.
They initially violate one precept
and are unable to repent.
Because they do not repent,
they become lax and let it spread,
discarding everything altogether,
like that monkey
who lost one bean
and discarded everything.
Once there was a man
walking on a road.
On the road, he found a golden weasel.
He was overjoyed
and held it in his bosom.
As he proceeded along the road,
he came to a river he wanted to cross.
He took off his clothes and placed them on the ground.
At that moment, the golden weasel turned into a poisonous snake.
The man pondered deeply:
"Even if the poisonous snake stings me to death,
I must carry it away."
His sincere intention caused a mystical change,
and it transformed back into gold.
A foolish person nearby saw the poisonous snake turn into a real treasure
and assumed it was always like that.
He then took a poisonous snake
and placed it inside his bosom.
He was immediately stung by the poisonous snake,
lost his life, and died.
Foolish people in the world are also like this.
Seeing good fortune,
they have no sincerity within.
They only cling to the Dharma for the sake of gain and support.
After death, they fall into evil realms,
like grasping a poisonous snake
and being stung to death.
Once there was a poor man
walking on the road.
On the road, he happened to find a bag of gold coins.
He was overjoyed
and immediately began to count them.
Before he could finish counting,
the owner of the gold suddenly appeared,
and took all the coins back.
The man then regretted not leaving quickly,
and his feelings of remorse were extremely painful.
Those who encounter the Buddha's Dharma are also like this.
Although they have the opportunity to encounter the Three Jewels,
the field of blessings,
they do not diligently practice good deeds.
Suddenly, their lives end,
and they fall into the three evil paths,
like that foolish man
who had his money taken away by its owner.
As the verse says:
"Today, managing this affair,
tomorrow, creating that affair,
delighting in attachments, not observing suffering,
unaware that the thief of death arrives.
Hastily managing many affairs,
ordinary people are all like this,
like those who count money,
their affairs are also like this."
Once there was a poor man with little wealth.
Seeing the very wealthy,
he desired to be equal to them.
Unable to be equal,
he wanted to throw the little wealth he had into the water.
Someone nearby said,
"Although this thing is small, it can sustain your life for several days.
Why discard it
and throw it into the water?"
Foolish people in the world are also like this.
Although they have left home
and gained a little support,
their hearts are filled with desires
and they are always dissatisfied.
They cannot become equal to those of high virtue
and obtain their support.
Seeing that those who have long been virtuous
are well-versed in the scriptures and have many offerings,
they desire to be equal to them.
Unable to be equal,
their hearts are filled with worry and suffering,
and they want to abandon the path,
like that foolish man
who, wanting to be equal to the wealthy,
discarded his own wealth.
Once there was a wet nurse
carrying a child on the road.
Walking along the road, she became tired and fell asleep, unaware.
At that time, a man
holding a ball of joy gave it to the child.
Having obtained it, the child craved its delicious flavor
and did not care for its possessions.
The man then immediately untied the child's chains, locks, necklaces, and clothing,
taking everything away completely.
*Bǐqiū* (monks) are also like this.
They delight in worldly affairs
and noisy places, greedy for small gains.
The thief of afflictions steals their merits, precepts, and jeweled necklaces,
like that child
who, craving a small taste,
had everything stolen by the thief.
Once there was an old woman
sleeping under a tree.
A bear was about to attack.
At that time, the old woman ran around the tree to escape,
and the bear chased after her.
It grabbed the tree with one hand
and tried to catch the old woman.
The old woman, in desperation,
immediately grabbed the tree and pinned the bear's two hands together,
so the bear could not move.
Another person came to that place.
The old woman said,
"You help me catch it, and we'll kill it and divide the meat."
That person believed the old woman's words
and immediately helped to catch it.
Once he had caught it,
the old woman immediately abandoned the bear and ran away.
The person was later trapped by the bear.
Such a foolish person is laughed at by the world.
Ordinary people are also like this.
Making various arguments
that are not well-reasoned,
their writing is cumbersome
and full of flaws.
They never finish them
and abandon them before dying.
Later people grasp them
wanting to explain them,
but they do not understand their meaning
and are instead trapped by them,
like that foolish person
who helped others catch the bear and was harmed himself.
Once there was a man
having an affair with another man's wife.
Before the affair was over,
the husband came home from outside.
The wife immediately sensed it
and stayed outside the door,
waiting for him to come out
so she could kill him.
The wife said to the man,
"My husband has become aware.
There is no way out
except through the *móní* (摩尼), which can let you out."
(*Móní*
in *Qí* (齊) language means water drain hole). She wanted the man to exit from the water drain.
That person misunderstood
and thought it was a móní zhū (摩尼珠),
searching for it everywhere
without knowing where it was.
He then said:
"If I don't see the móní zhū (摩尼珠),
I will never leave."
In a short while, he was killed because of it.
Ordinary people are also like this.
Someone says:
"In the cycle of birth and death,
there is impermanence,
suffering, emptiness,
and no self.
By leaving the two extremes of permanence and annihilation,
and abiding in the Middle Way,
by passing through this,
one can attain liberation."
Ordinary people misunderstand
and seek whether the world has boundaries or not, and whether sentient beings have a self or not.
In the end, they cannot contemplate the principle of the Middle Way,
and suddenly their lives end.
They are killed by impermanence,
and fall into the three evil paths,
like that foolish person
who sought the móní (摩尼)
and was harmed by others.
Once, there were two pigeons, male and female,
sharing the same nest.
When the autumn fruits ripened, they filled their nest with fruits.
Later, when the fruits dried and shrunk,
only half a nest remained.
The male, angry, said to the female:
"Gathering fruits is hard work.
You ate them all alone,
only half remains."
The female pigeon replied:
"I did not eat them alone,
the fruits shrank by themselves."
The male pigeon did not believe her,
and said in anger:
"If you didn't eat them alone,
how could they have shrunk?"
He then pecked the female pigeon to death.
Not many days later,
heavy rain fell,
and the fruits became wet
and returned to their original state.
When the male pigeon saw this,
he felt regret:
"She didn't really eat them,
I killed her wrongly."
He then cried out, calling for the female pigeon,
"Where have you gone?"
Ordinary people are also like this,
with reversed thoughts in their minds,
falsely seeking sensual pleasures
without contemplating impermanence,
violating serious precepts,
regretting it afterwards,
but what can be done?
Later, they only lament,
like that foolish pigeon.
Once, there was a craftsman,
working for the king,
unable to bear the hardship.
He falsely claimed to be blind
and was thus freed from hardship.
Another craftsman heard of this
and wanted to blind himself
to avoid the hard labor.
Someone said:
"Why do you destroy yourself?
You only suffer in vain."
Such a foolish person is laughed at by the world.
Ordinary people are also like this,
for a little fame and profit, they deliberately lie
and break pure precepts.
When their bodies die and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil paths,
like that foolish person
who, for a little gain,
blinded himself.
Once, there were two people traveling together in a wilderness.
One person had a wool blanket.
On the road, he was robbed by thieves.
The other person escaped
and ran into the grass.
The one who lost the blanket had previously wrapped a gold coin at the head of the blanket.
He then said to the thief:
"This garment is only worth one gold coin.
I now ask to redeem it for one gold coin."
The thief said:
"Where is the gold coin now?"
He then untied the head of the blanket to show it,
and said to the thief:
"This is real gold.
If you don't believe my words,
there is a good goldsmith in this grass
who you can ask."
The thief, having seen it,
took the garment as well.
Such a foolish person lost both the blanket and the gold coin,
losing his own benefit
and also causing the other to lose.
Ordinary people are also like this.
They cultivate the practices of the path
and perform various meritorious deeds,
but are robbed by the thieves of afflictions,
losing their good dharmas
and forfeiting all merits.
Not only do they lose their own benefit,
but they also cause others to lose their progress on the path.
When their bodies break and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil paths,
like that foolish person
who lost everything for both.
Once, there was a young child
playing on land
and caught a large turtle.
Intending to kill it
but not knowing how,
he asked someone:
"How can I kill it?"
Someone said:
"Just throw it into the water
and it can be killed immediately."
At that time, the child, believing his words, threw it into the water.
The turtle, having reached the water,
immediately ran away.
Ordinary people are also like this.
Wanting to guard the six senses
and cultivate all kinds of merits
but not understanding the means,
they ask someone:
"What causes and conditions will lead to liberation?"
Heretical outsiders, the heavenly demon Bō Xún (波旬), and evil teachers tell them:
"Just indulge in the six objects of sense and indulge your desires to the fullest.
If you do as I say,
you will surely attain liberation."
Such foolish people do not carefully consider
and follow their words.
When their bodies break and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil paths,
like the child who threw the turtle into the water.
This treatise is what I have created,
combining joyous and humorous speech.
It mostly diminishes true and honest speech;
observe whether its meaning is appropriate or not.
Like bitter poison,
mixed with rock candy,
the medicine destroys the disease;
this treatise is also like that.
Jesting in the true Dharma
is like that mad medicine.
The Buddha's true Dharma is peaceful and still,
illuminating the world.
Like taking a purgative,
and using ghee to moisten the body,
I now use this meaning
to reveal that stillness.
Like the Ā Qié Tuó (阿伽陀) medicine,
wrapped in tree leaves,
after taking the medicine and applying it to the poison,
the tree leaves are discarded.
Humorous speech is like the wrapping leaves,
the true meaning is within it.
The wise take the true meaning;
humorous speech should then be discarded.
Venerable Sēng Qié Sī Nà (僧伽斯那) completes the composition of the Málà (鬘, garland) of Foolishness.
